problems.source_says: The abstract explicitly claims random assignment, and Section 3.3 says participants were assigned through simple random sampling, but that same methods section labels the design quasi-experimental. No further allocation description resolves this conflict. The form already acknowledges the uncertainty, but randomized=yes and field_rct can represent only the authors' disputed claim, not a confirmed randomized design. This conflict also does not establish that assignment was nonrandom.
problems.quote: The study employed a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design (see Figure 1) and adopted a mixed-methods research approach.
problems.locator: PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Section 3.3, first and final sentences; contrasting random-assignment claim in the abstract on PDF p. 1 (journal p. 79). Complete markdown read, including references and author biography; no appendix or further allocation explanation is included.

confirmed.statement: The abstract explicitly states that 76 students were randomly assigned to control and experimental groups.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 1 (journal p. 79), abstract, third sentence.

confirmed.statement: The methods explicitly say participants were assigned to either group through simple random sampling; the problem is conflicting design descriptions, not an absence of random-assignment language.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Section 3.3, final sentence.

confirmed.statement: The study has separate experimental and control groups, with 38 students in each and pre/post measurement in both. It is not a within-person crossover, so randomized condition order is not applicable.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 83), Section 3.1; PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Section 3.3 and Figure 1, visually checked.

confirmed.statement: The experimental arm received a five-week, ten-hour GenAI storytelling workshop, with two 60-minute sessions per week in the school computer lab and instructor-designed prompt banks.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 83), Sections 3.1-3.2; PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Section 3.2, paragraph below Figure 1.

confirmed.statement: Table 1 specifies text generation, prompt crafting and outline building using GenAI tools, creation and revision of visuals, and AI music generation, supporting the generative-AI classification.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 7 (journal p. 85), Table 1, weeks 2-4; checked using PDF text and PyMuPDF table extraction.

confirmed.statement: Students used AI-generated suggestions to develop their own stories; comparing AI- and human-generated stories was only one introductory activity, not the experimental contrast.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 7 (journal p. 85), Table 1, weeks 1-5; PDF pp. 9-10 (journal pp. 87-88), RQ2, Cognitive, Behavioral and Ethical Domains.

confirmed.statement: The control group continued conventional English lessons without exposure to any AI tools, matching the no-AI comparison arm.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 83), Section 3.1, first paragraph.

confirmed.statement: Figure 1 labels both the pre-test and post-test storytelling tasks as No AI Help; the AI exposure was the intervening workshop.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Figure 1, pre-test, intervention/control and post-test boxes, visually checked.

confirmed.statement: The intervention description does not identify a product, model or version; leaving ai_tool.name_model null is appropriate.
confirmed.locator: PDF pp. 5-7 (journal pp. 83-85), Sections 3.1-3.2 and Table 1; complete markdown review found no intervention-specific identification elsewhere.

summary: The paper explicitly claims random assignment, but its methods also call the study quasi-experimental and do not resolve the contradictory design descriptions. Generative-AI assistance for students' own storytelling and a no-AI control are supported, but criterion 1 remains unclear.
